name: Diaphragmatic Plication
overview: Surgical reinforcement of paralyzed or weakened diaphragm

pimpingQuestions.question: The diaphragm develops from four embryologic sources. What are they, and which corresponds to the central tendon?
pimpingQuestions.answer: 1) Septum transversum (central tendon — the main embryologic component), 2) Pleuroperitoneal membranes (close the pleuroperitoneal canals), 3) Dorsal mesentery of the esophagus (contributes the crura), 4) Body wall mesoderm (peripheral muscular rim from cervical myotomes C3-C5 — this is why the phrenic nerve descends from C3-C5 to innervate a thoracoabdominal structure). Eventration occurs when the muscular component fails to develop properly.

pimpingQuestions.question: What is the 'sniff test' for diagnosing diaphragmatic paralysis, and what does a positive test look like?
pimpingQuestions.answer: Fluoroscopic or ultrasound observation during quick inspiratory sniff through the nose. Normal: both hemidiaphragms descend with sniffing. Positive test (paradoxical motion): the paralyzed hemidiaphragm rises ≥2cm during sniffing (pulled upward by the negative intrathoracic pressure generated by the functioning contralateral hemidiaphragm). Ultrasound is now preferred over fluoroscopy (no radiation) — M-mode ultrasound measures diaphragmatic excursion quantitatively. A difference of >50% between sides confirms unilateral paralysis.

pimpingQuestions.question: What are the inferior phrenic arteries, and how are they preserved during diaphragmatic plication?
pimpingQuestions.answer: The right and left inferior phrenic arteries are typically the first branches of the abdominal aorta (or may arise from the celiac trunk). They supply the majority of the diaphragmatic dome, running along the inferior surface and branching radially. During VATS plication (approaching from above), these arteries are not directly visualized — the plication sutures pass through the full thickness of the attenuated diaphragm but should avoid the central hiatal region where the inferior phrenic vessels are largest to prevent hemorrhage into the abdomen.

pimpingQuestions.question: What is the expected FEV1 improvement after plication, and which patients benefit most versus least?
pimpingQuestions.answer: Mean FEV1 improvement: 15-20%. FVC improvement: 20-25%. Patients who benefit most: symptomatic dyspnea on exertion with documented paradoxical motion, BMI <35, and no underlying lung disease. Patients who benefit least: bilateral phrenic nerve paralysis (both diaphragms paralyzed — bilateral plication has higher morbidity and limited benefit; these patients may need long-term ventilatory support), morbid obesity (persistent restriction), and advanced COPD (dyspnea is multifactorial).

pimpingQuestions.question: What is the long-term durability of diaphragmatic plication, and what causes plication failure?
pimpingQuestions.answer: Long-term success: >85% maintain symptomatic improvement at 5-10 years. Plication failure (15%): suture pullthrough (most common — the attenuated diaphragm muscle is thin and may not hold sutures), progressive neuromuscular disease (ALS, myasthenia), and recurrent phrenic nerve injury. Pledgets or felt strips reinforce the plication sutures in severely attenuated tissue. Re-do plication is technically feasible but has lower success rates (60-70%) due to scarring and tissue quality.
